payload.title: Why EREVs Could Narrow the Maintenance Gap With Full EVs
payload.excerpt: Xiaomi’s new SkyNomad EREVs point to unusually long oil-change intervals, showing how range-extender vehicles may reduce one of their biggest ownership disadvantages.
payload.content:
Extended-range electric vehicles promise a practical compromise: most day-to-day driving can happen on battery power, while a gasoline engine remains available to generate electricity when longer trips demand it. The trade-off has always been obvious, though. Adding an internal-combustion engine also adds oil, fluids, moving parts and another maintenance schedule.

Recent servicing guidance for Xiaomi’s SkyNomad N70 and N90 suggests that gap may be smaller than many buyers expect. According to InsideEVs, the two extended-range crossovers use a 1.5-liter turbocharged four-cylinder engine as a range extender. Xiaomi’s published plan calls for the first oil service after one year or 10,000 kilometers, followed by intervals of up to three years or 30,000 kilometers of engine operation.

Why an EREV engine can age differently

The key is utilization. In a conventional car, the engine is responsible for nearly every kilometer. An EREV can spend substantial time moving on stored battery energy instead. If the owner regularly charges the vehicle and the gasoline engine runs only occasionally, engine wear does not accumulate at the same rate as total vehicle mileage.

That distinction matters because maintenance intervals tied to engine use can be much longer than buyers might infer from the odometer alone. InsideEVs also notes that Li Auto has adopted similarly long service intervals for some of its EREV models, suggesting this is not necessarily an isolated experiment.

Long intervals do not mean zero maintenance

It would be a mistake to conclude that an EREV becomes mechanically equivalent to a battery-only EV. The combustion system is still present and still requires appropriate servicing. Time also matters even when mileage is low, because oil and other fluids can degrade while a vehicle sits or runs its engine infrequently.

The more useful takeaway is narrower: manufacturers may be able to design the range-extender system around intermittent operation rather than treating it like a conventional powertrain. InsideEVs reports that Li Auto has made engine-design changes and used specialized oil to support longer intervals. For Xiaomi, the exact engineering behind the extended schedule is less clear, although the report notes a special low-viscosity oil associated with Shell.

What this changes for buyers

For consumers comparing a full EV with an EREV, maintenance should be evaluated by actual service requirements rather than by simply counting the number of powertrain components. A range-extender vehicle is mechanically more complex, but that complexity does not automatically translate into frequent servicing if the combustion engine operates only a small fraction of the time.

The biggest question is whether long service intervals remain practical over years of real-world ownership across different climates, driving patterns and charging habits. Xiaomi’s schedule is a manufacturer recommendation, not yet a long-term fleet study. Buyers should therefore separate the documented service interval from broader claims about lifetime reliability or total ownership cost.

The larger signal

EREVs are increasingly positioned as a bridge between combustion cars and battery-only EVs. Their appeal depends on preserving as much of the electric-driving experience as possible while retaining a backup energy source for longer journeys. If manufacturers can also reduce the maintenance penalty of carrying that gasoline engine, one of the format’s clearest disadvantages becomes less significant.

That does not make an EREV maintenance-free. It does make the ownership equation more interesting. The relevant metric may no longer be simply whether a vehicle has an engine, but how often that engine actually has to work.

Source

  • InsideEVs: EREVs Can Apparently Be Almost As Low-Maintenance As Full EVs
